scenarios.title: The aged balance trapped in a print file
An application inventory with hand-typed URLs
Failed orders hidden in the logs
The wrong bar code caught at import
scenarios.lede:
A catalogue export carries EAN-13 bar codes, some of them wrong. No built-in transformer computes the check digit.
- the hub's operator drops a Kotlin script
- the manifest names it, carrying no code
- a draft that does not compile is refused at validation
- every code gets a verdict at import.

scenarios.title: A CFONB statement with the sign hidden in the last digit
A CRM export with broken accents and wrong emails
The €240,000 deal that confirms itself during dinner
A delivery date each warehouse works out differently
scenarios.lede:
The promised date = order date plus N working days. But each warehouse counts its own way:
- Lyon, in France: 3 days, two inventory days;
- Liège, in Belgium: 5 days, other holidays.
The operator writes the rule once; the integrator sets it per warehouse.

scenarios.title: k8s forgot, lumnik remembers: who crashed last night?
scenarios.lede:
Kubernetes keeps its events for one hour. A deployment repaired at dawn has no history by morning:
- a new pod, Running, 0 restarts;
- no Warning event left.
lumnik reads the events while they exist and keeps them; Ask still answers when kubectl no longer knows.

scenarios.title: k8s is burning, k9s says Running: which pod first?
An unapproved hotfix in k8s prod: the pipeline stops.
One order status, fourteen spellings
scenarios.lede:
Fifteen years of hand entry left EC, Livré, LIV, ANNUL… in the ERP's order export. lumnik does not touch the ERP:
- a Workflow declares four statuses and their spellings
- every import re-checks the column.

scenarios.title: A flat EDI file from an ERP: fixed-width order lines, read without a mapping tool.
scenarios.lede: A manufacturer exchanges flat files with its logistics partner, one folder per partner, one prefix per exchange type. No separator: every field has its place and its width, a header line first, ISO-8859-1, and sometimes no line end after the last line. The partner wants the order lines as columns.

scenarios.title: Four EDI files for a single order line
scenarios.lede:
A manufacturer and its logistics partner exchange four flat files around one order line: the order, the acknowledgement, the confirmed date, the delivery note. Sales administration asks, line by line:
- never acknowledged?
- confirmed but not delivered?
- delivered in another quantity?

scenarios.title: An EDIFACT ORDERS message: one line, split into segments, the escaped apostrophe kept.
scenarios.lede: Retail and industry still exchange EDIFACT: a buyer's ORDERS message, often written on one single line, its segments ended by an apostrophe, its elements split by + and :. An apostrophe in a label is written ?'. The buyer wants to read the message segment by segment.

scenarios.title: One customer, two systems, no shared identifier.
scenarios.lede: An ERP, a CRM, one Entity. Email matches the records; a shared mailbox opens an ambiguity. lumnik does not pick: a person decides, and the decision holds on replay.

scenarios.title: An established customer does not change records in silence.
scenarios.lede: Yesterday, CRM contact CC-42 and ERP account AC-700 both meant Nova Pumps. Today its email points to Helios Valves. lumnik does not move the contact: it makes it ambiguous, and a person decides.

scenarios.title: An Excel export with merged cells: every line with its region and client.
scenarios.lede: Sales send a monthly Excel report: one group per client, the region and the client in merged cells, a subtotal under each group. Saved as CSV, a merged cell keeps its value on the group's first row only; the rows below are empty. Sales want every line with its region and client.

scenarios.title: The export that lies: an unreadable line does not pass in silence.
scenarios.lede: An ERP exports its article catalogue every night as one file. A label holds the delimiter, unquoted. lumnik sets the line aside with its raw values, removes nothing from the catalogue while it is unreadable, and closes the dead letter only on the run that really read it again.

scenarios.title: A critical incident, no technician
scenarios.lede:
A CMMS exports its incidents as CSV. The conveyor on the gummy candy line has stopped, with no technician. The CMMS warns no one.
- a Workflow tracks each incident's status
- a Process flags the critical unassigned incident
- one decision only; the assignment moves it forward.

scenarios.title: A claim form's lists, without exposing the CRM's GraphQL.
scenarios.lede: Claim type and subtype live in a CRM that speaks GraphQL. lumnik ingests it page by page, turns it into a canonical entity, and a small BFF serves the form stable REST JSON: the CRM's schema never becomes a browser contract.

scenarios.title: The catalogue reaches the partner in their format, not ours.
scenarios.lede: Two ERP CSV files, products and categories, are joined in the hub and delivered to S3 in a partner's format: French headers, semicolons, decimal commas, recoded statuses, a masked internal reference. A receipt proves the delivered bytes.

scenarios.title: An unreadable amount does not get in: the invoice waits, fixed at the source.
scenarios.lede: A supplier-invoice export carries two mistyped amounts and a test invoice. Instead of writing invoices without an amount, the hub sets them aside with the row as it was read. The test invoice is discarded, the source is fixed, and each letter is closed by the run that brought the right row.

scenarios.title: One product record, two databases: PostgreSQL and Oracle stay where they are.
scenarios.lede: Products live in PostgreSQL, their categories in Oracle. Two jdbc connectors read them without writing to either, and one entity joins them: 40,234 products, each with its category when there is one.

scenarios.title: At 23:15, the same number does not mean the same thing everywhere.
scenarios.lede: Three meters publish their power on Kafka. Lyon draws 18.7 kW, the Grenoble laboratory 28.4 kW. Only Lyon breaks its night threshold: one decision, one email to its owner, and a Grafana dashboard that follows the three states.

scenarios.title: An open door, a silent sensor
scenarios.lede:
Sensors publish freezer door states on Kafka. FZ-17 opens and goes quiet. FZ-18 opens and closes again.
- a Workflow watches the silence
- one alert only, for the door left open past one minute
- it names the laboratory and the owner.

scenarios.title: A frozen ERP feeds a real Grafana dashboard, with no extra connector.
scenarios.lede: The ERP exports its sales and catalogue as CSV. lumnik joins them, and Grafana reads the entity through a read-only PostgreSQL login bound to its tenant. Monday: EUR 10,450. On Tuesday the export changes: EUR 14,200, and the changed sale appears once.

scenarios.title: A marketplace's orders, one line per item to pick: model, colour, size.
scenarios.lede: The marketplace export gives one line per order, the items packed into one cell, and an item reference that packs model, colour and size in turn. Logistics wants one line per item, to count what to take out of stock. The manifest splits the order, then the reference, and refuses a file whose column was renamed.

scenarios.title: One hub, one app per métier.
scenarios.lede: Maintenance and purchasing share an ERP where everyone sees everything. On one hub, lumnik composes one app per métier; a technician whose only role is scope:maintenance sees its app, its orders and its decisions, and every purchasing door answers with a refusal.

scenarios.title: Auditing how long orders stay in each status
scenarios.lede:
The ERP keeps only today's status: In progress yesterday, Delivered today. Nothing on the wait in between. The ERP cannot be changed.
- a Workflow follows each order by its key
- each status change enters a journal, dated
- an order that stays still too long alerts
- the journal says how long each order stayed in each state.

scenarios.title: The question Ask refuses to answer: a margin with no cost, a "best" with no criterion.
scenarios.lede: A purchasing director asks a year of supplier orders questions in French. Three get their figure, with the SQL that produced it. Three others have no answer in this data: a margin with no cost price, a best supplier with no criterion, delays with no delivery date. Ask refuses them instead of inventing a figure someone would repeat in a meeting.

scenarios.title: "Et SUP-004 ?": a follow-up question, answered as the whole question.
scenarios.lede: A buyer asks how many orders were cancelled, then "Et pour le fournisseur SUP-003 ?", then "Et SUP-004 ?". Nobody retypes the question. Ask reads each follow-up with the question before it, answers the full question and shows the one it understood.

scenarios.title: Question 40,000 products, with the SQL shown.
scenarios.lede: Two CSV exports, one entity, an app reduced to chat. The question becomes a read-only query; the answer shows its SQL.

scenarios.title: 40,000 products, browsed page by page.
scenarios.lede: Two CSV exports, two entities, two linked views, one app. The hub serves the catalogue 50 rows at a time; the PWA never loads more.

scenarios.title: Search 40,000 products, facets included.
scenarios.lede: Two CSV exports, one entity, a SearchIndex, an app reduced to search. The hub indexes the declared columns; the PWA filters by facet.

scenarios.title: One unexpected value in 500: that line dead-lettered, the other 499 written.
scenarios.lede: A hand-typed goods receipt: 500 lines, quantities written "12,5 kg" or "3 pce". An operator's Kotlin script reads them into a number and a unit. Line 317 says "env. 4 kg". What happens to the other 499?

scenarios.title: The API that only sends what changed: an order modified while it is being read is not lost.
scenarios.lede: An order API can answer "what changed since this date". lumnik reads it in full once, then each night only what moved. An order modified while a run is still reading later pages could have slipped between two nights: the next run starts a little before its last mark, and picks it up.

scenarios.title: The partner's API loses a page, the run does not lie.
scenarios.lede: A partner publishes 2,400 partners and their count. One night a page of 100 vanishes; the count stays right. lumnik compares what it read with the total the source declares: the run fails naming the endpoint and both numbers, instead of turning green.

scenarios.title: A Spring app behind a proxy: name the framework, key on the SKU.
The SaaS behind OAuth2: 30-second tokens, a 40-second run, no page lost.
scenarios.lede: The ERP no longer moves, but some orders arrive through a recent SaaS. That SaaS no longer takes a fixed token: it hands out a client id and a secret, and wants a short-lived token on every call. lumnik asks for the token, renews it before it expires, absorbs a key rotation in the middle of a run, and says why when the secret is revoked, without ever showing it.

scenarios.title: SAP ORDERS05 IDocs as a flat file: every order line with its purchase order.
scenarios.lede: A customer's SAP sends its orders as ORDERS05 IDocs, written to a flat file: one EDI_DC40 control record per IDoc, then fixed-width data records. The PO number sits in E2EDK02, the quantity in the item E2EDP01, our article in the E2EDP19 that follows it. The order desk wants one row per order line.

scenarios.title: The carrier's SFTP drop: every night read, put away, and nothing on trust.
scenarios.lede: A carrier drops livraisons.csv on its SFTP server every night, always under the same name. lumnik reads a night of the same size again, puts each night away under its own name, says on the run a file it could not archive, and refuses a server whose key has changed.

scenarios.title: The rule changed on 1 January: every order says which version computed it.
scenarios.lede: The shipping fee is computed by a Kotlin script the hub's operator provides: free shipping from 150.00 in December, from 200.00 from January. The operator replaces the script. Months later, an auditor asks why an order of 172.50 shipped free in December and paid shipping in January.

scenarios.title: The CRM's SOAP desk: each service read its own way, nothing read twice.
scenarios.lede: A 2000s CRM exposes its data through custom SOAP web services: a case's actions in one call, a customer's opportunities page by page on a page number. The password travels inside the envelope. lumnik reads each one the way it reads, carries the service's Fault verbatim, and never sends the same request twice.

scenarios.title: A changed bank account the SIEM never sees
scenarios.lede:
The ERP exports its suppliers as CSV. It emits no event. A bank-account change goes unnoticed until the next payment.
- lumnik rereads the export every minute
- a signed decision goes to the SIEM by webhook
- the SIEM alerts on the account that changes
- the inbox never shows the account.

scenarios.title: The supplier file sent to EDI: ASCII, upper case, 35 characters, a stable identifier.
scenarios.lede: Purchasing feeds an EDI platform that requires names in ASCII, upper case, 35 characters at most, and one identifier per supplier. The ERP export has accents, long legal names, inactive suppliers, and an id column holding N/A, 0 or nothing. The EDI's constraint is declared once in the manifest.

scenarios.title: Two systems, one member: each the reference for its own fields.
scenarios.lede: A mutual insurer keeps its members in its contract system and in its portal. Fused with one source order, one of the two is always wrong. lumnik lets each column name its reference source, and keeps every dispute visible until the source settles it.

scenarios.title: Two customers, one hub, one table: each reads only its own rows.
scenarios.lede: Two integrators of two customers apply the same files to the same hub. Same connector, same entity, same table. Each loads its orders, under the same numbers. Each reads, asks and counts: it sees only its own.

scenarios.title: The zombie system: thirty years of work orders, the box switched off, the hub still answers.
scenarios.lede: A CMMS replaced years ago stays on for a handful of compliance reads a year: the licence, the box, and the one person who can restart it. lumnik reads it one last time, archives what it read under a single digest, then the box is switched off. The next run says why it fails, the pause stops the schedule, and the hub gives back the same bytes as before.
